fetched_contents.text: Estimation of typical agricultural machinery emissions in China: Real-world emission factors and inventories Introduction Characterized by a high engine power and low fuel consumption, diesel engines have been widely applied in agricultural machinery (Liu et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019a; Triantafyllopoulos et al., 2019). According to the 2020 China Agricultural Machinery Industry Yearbook, as of 2019, the total mechanical power of agricultural machinery in China reached 1027.6 million kW, of which diesel engine power accounted for 77.6%. The 2019 China Mobile Source Environmental Management Annual Report revealed that in 2018, the nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions generated by tractors and combine harvesters accounted for 59.0% and 4.8% of the total NOx emissions from agricultural machinery, respectively; moreover, the particulate matter (PM) emissions produced by tractors and combine harvesters accounted for 60.1% and 3.4% of the total PM emissions from agricultural machinery (MEE, 2019), respectively. However, the emissions of carbon monoxide (CO), hydrocarbons (HC), NOx and PM generated by agricultural machinery (Larsson and Hansson, 2011; Zhang et al., 2020a; Lovarelli and Bacenetti, 2019) are the culprits of air pollution (Zhang et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Bacenetti et al., 2018) and endanger human health (Gonzalez-de-Soto et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019b; Lelieveld et al., 2015). Therefore, research on the emissions of nonroad agricultural machinery is required. Current studies of emissions produced by nonroad mobile agricultural machinery (Siedlecki et al., 2017; Velmurugan et al., 2020; Janulevič ius and Č iplien ė , 2018) are usually conducted by performing bench tests and portable emission measurement system (PEMS)-based tests. However, the emission levels of nonroad agricultural machinery under real-world working conditions cannot be fully portrayed due to the limitations of the bench test cycle (Ettl et al., 2016; Pirjola et al., 2017; Desouza et al., 2020). PEMS-based methods are utilized by experts and scholars at home and abroad to further study the emissions of agricultural machinery under real-world working conditions. Rymaniak et al. (2020) tested the emissions from typical agricultural tractors and found that their fuel consumption increased as engine speed and load increased. Fu et al. (2013), who measured 12 agricultural tractors with different emission standards (China Ⅱ, China Ⅰ and pre-China Ⅰ) using the PEMS device, found that the CO, HC and NOx fuel consumption-based emission factors were lower than those in the idling and moving modes. Pang et al. (2020) tested the emissions of 9 tractors used for different purposes (field transportation, rototilling, fertilizing, straw chopping and straw mulching). The CO, NO and PM2.5 emission rates of a rototilling tractor were obviously higher than those of other tractors used for field transportation, fertilizing, straw chopping and straw mulching. Ge et al. (2013) analysed emissions from combine harvesters and showed that emissions from grain combine harvesters were higher than those from corn combine harvesters. Yu et al. (2023) studied carbonyl compounds emitted from agricultural machinery using PEMS and showed that the emission factors of carbonyl compounds from China II medium tractors were 2.56 and 4.83 times higher than those of China II large tractors and China II combine harvesters, respectively. Notably, due to the lack of engine performance data, the researchers mentioned above tested the emissions of agricultural machinery under real-world operating conditions, although most of them focused on analysing fuel consumption-based emission factors. The emission factors are considered the basic data for compiling the emission inventory, which serves as the basis and prerequisite for emission control (Fu et al., 2014). However, due to a lack of official or reliable fuel consumption statistical data, empirical data are applied to the emission inventory, which will substantially affect the accuracy of the estimated results. In 2014, the Ministry of Ecology and Environment of the People's Republic of China (MEE) (2014a) issued the Guidelines for the Compilation of Non-Road Mobiles Air Pollutant Emission Inventory (Trial) (hereinafter referred to the guidelines), which provide guidance for local governments to establish off-road mobile source emission inventories. Based on the guidelines, a power-based emission inventory is the preferred method to calculate off-road mobile source emissions because of its relatively higher accuracy. However, unified power-based emission factors from the guidelines are provided, regardless of machinery types, which will introduce uncertainty when calculating the emissions from individual machinery types. Hou et al. (2019) applied a power-based approach to estimate the emissions of typical agricultural machinery in Beijing and reported that the CO, HC, NOx and PM emissions decreased by 63.1%, 62.9%, 72.1% and 74.7%, respectively, from 2006 to 2016. Lang et al. (2018) used the statistics of the sowing time and harvesting time for wheat, corn and rice collected, and built a national-level emission inventory of agricultural machinery of China in 2014. However, due to lack of real-world engine performance and emission data, the emission factors from the above studies are derived from guideline-recommended values or estimated tested values. In addition, the power-based emission inventory method does not fully reflect the cross-regional operating performance when machinery moves from one region to another region, further weakening the spatiotemporal emission accuracy on small scales. Therefore, a more practical method is needed to determine the emission time and spatial distribution at different scales. fetched_contents.text: Simulated Farm Fieldwork, Energy Consumption and Related Greenhouse Gas Emissions in Canada Abstract The amount of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions that can be attributed to agricultural machinery management was analysed using computer simulation of farm power requirements, machine hours and fuel consumption. The ‘Farm Fieldwork and Fossil Fuel Energy and Emissions’ (F4E2) model optimised tractor and harvester power P. To minimise P for a single tractor for spring tillage and sowing, the model budgets available spring work time in half-day increments and adjusts implement widths to match. Other field operations in the model are powered by a tractor derived for spring. Emissions of GHG were estimated for ploughing, discing and sowing operations in springs, along with autumn harvesting, cultivation for weeds, spreading manure and sprying for pests. A grain trailer and a swather were considered as part of harvesting. Farm site estimates were extrapolated to regional and national scales with appropriate and available Canadian Census and farm survey data. Fuel consumption and GHG emission factors for petrol and diesel fuels were also analysed. Fuel efficiency and proper matching of equipment to tractors were important factors. Canada's 1996 Farm Energy Use Survey (FEUS) provided useful validation to the F4E2 energy consumption estimates. The model estimate of 71·6 PJ of diesel energy for 1996 was within 1% of the 72·0 PJ of diesel fuel energy that FEUS attributes to farm machinery for Canada. The 1990 Kyoto baseline estimate of GHG emissions was 6·5 Tg of CO2 equivalent from both diesel and petrol for farm field operations in Canada. Introduction Canada's greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction target resulting from the 1997 international gathering in Kyoto, Japan, 6% below 1990 emissions by 2008 to 2012, will affect all sectors. On-farm use of fuel in 1996 accounted for almost one-third of all carbon dioxide emissions (both fossil and organic sources) attributed to farmland in Canada (Janzen et al., 1999). Of the total fossil fuel consumed by Canadian farm operations and farm family life, about 45% was used for farm fieldwork (Tremblay, 2000). There has been no analysis of how farm level decisions about specific field operations and machinery selections affected this fuel use. The main objective of this paper is to estimate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions associated with both past and present farm fieldwork to produce annual field crops. Since 1990, the baseline year for Kyoto reduction targets, Canadian crop production practices have undergone major changes. Policy formulation must reflect these changes, identify GHG reductions that are still needed and reward progress already made before reduction incentives such as taxes or tax breaks are implemented. Therefore, pre-1990 emissions need to be assessed with a methodology that can be updated for current farm machinery management such as changing land use and tillage practices. The second objective is to develop a methodology that can relate these GHG emissions to machinery management decisions at the farm level, where environmental responsibility ultimately falls (Kutzbach, 2000). Machinery selections, hours of use and energy consumed on typical Canadian farms can guide farm operations and drive economic analysis of measures that reduce GHG emissions. As well, comparing power estimates with Census of Canada farm tractor statistics provides an independent means of verifying farm fuel consumption estimates, including both the number and sizes of tractors on typical farms. Toward these objectives, the ‘Farm Fieldwork and Fossil Fuel Energy and Emissions’ (F4E2) model was created to analyse mobile fuels. China-specific agricultural machinery emissions profile

The evidence points to tractors and combine harvesters as the dominant machinery categories in China’s agricultural emissions inventory. A 2022 study tested 39 typical agricultural machines in China, specifically 30 tractors and 9 corn combine harvesters, under real-world working conditions using PEMS devices [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that tractors and combine harvesters together account for most of China’s agricultural machinery emissions, with tractors responsible for 59.0% of NOx emissions and 60.1% of PM emissions from agricultural machinery in 2018, while combine harvesters accounted for 4.8% of NOx and 3.4% of PM emissions in the same year [N1-F1]. This suggests that tractors are the largest contributors, but combine harvesters remain significant, especially in harvesting operations.

Fuel use and engine efficiency by equipment category are tied closely to emissions intensity. The evidence indicates that diesel engines are widespread in agricultural machinery because they are characterized by high engine power and low fuel consumption [N1-F1]. The same source reports that the 2019 China Agricultural Machinery Industry Yearbook showed diesel engine power accounted for 77.6% of total mechanical power in China’s agricultural machinery fleet [N1-F1]. This implies a strong reliance on diesel fuel, which is consistent with the high fuel consumption and emissions observed in tractors. The evidence also highlights that emissions vary by operation type: for example, a rototilling tractor produced significantly higher CO, NO, and PM2.5 emission rates than tractors used for field transportation, fertilizing, straw chopping, and straw mulching [N1-F1]. Similarly, grain combine harvesters were found to emit more than corn combine harvesters [N1-F1]. These differences suggest that engine efficiency and operating load matter, with higher-intensity operations leading to worse emissions performance.

Seasonal variation in operation intensity and emissions is less directly specified in the evidence, but the context provided by the peak agricultural season is important. The evidence on seasonal activity patterns in China is thin; it mainly points to May 5th as Lixia, the seventh solar term, signaling peak growth season in early summer [N4-R3]. This is useful as background but not sufficient to establish exact seasonal patterns for agricultural machinery. Still, the broader emissions literature implies that agricultural operations intensify during harvest and planting windows, which would naturally increase operational hours and emissions. The 2014 study used sowing and harvesting times for wheat, corn, and rice to build a national-level agricultural machinery emission inventory [N1-F1], indicating that the timing of fieldwork is a central driver of emissions variation. The real-world PEMS-based testing in China suggests that emissions under actual working conditions can differ significantly from bench-test results, reinforcing that seasonality and operational conditions are critical [N1-F1].

Overall, the China-specific profile is dominated by tractors and combine harvesters, powered mostly by diesel engines, with emissions varying by equipment category and operation type. Seasonal variation is implied by the timing of planting and harvesting, but the evidence provided does not give a detailed seasonal emissions profile for agricultural machinery alone [N1-F1; N4-R3].

The evidence for road vehicle emissions in China emphasizes a large and diverse fleet, with fuel distribution and seasonal behavior shaped by vehicle type, fuel type, and regional traffic patterns. One source classifies vehicles into six categories: motorcycles, private cars, light-duty vehicles, buses, trucks, and rural vehicles, and two fuel types: gasoline and diesel [N2-R2]. Another study reports that China IV vehicles have the highest emission contribution rates, ranging from 32.5% to 44.9%, and notes that emissions peak in winter and are lowest in summer [N2-R5]. These findings together suggest a fleet composition skewed toward older, more polluting vehicles and a strong seasonal pattern.

Fleet composition and fuel distribution by vehicle type are best supported by the vehicle-category breakdown and the mention of China IV vehicles as dominant contributors [N2-R2][N2-R5]. The evidence also implies that rural vehicles are part of the broader on-road fleet and may contribute differently from urban categories, though the exact proportions are not quantified here [N2-R2]. Fuel-wise, the evidence indicates that diesel vehicles are important, especially among older vehicle classes, while gasoline vehicles are also a major component of the fleet. The seasonal study also notes that emissions peak in winter and decline in summer, indicating that winter conditions and heavier traffic loads likely increase emissions [N2-R5].

Seasonal trends in road traffic and emissions are best described as winter peak and summer trough, with the evidence explicitly stating that emissions peak in winter and are lowest in summer [N2-R5]. Another source on China’s vehicle emissions notes that seasonal vehicle emission rates vary by fuel type during holiday and non-holiday periods, though the holiday/non-holiday framing is less directly comparable to the peak agricultural season [N2-R1]. A separate source on road traffic injuries in China reports that RTIs were highest in summer and autumn and lowest in February, with rural areas and men being disproportionately affected [N7-R4]. While this is about injuries rather than emissions, it reinforces that traffic intensity and risk vary seasonally and regionally, which matters for emissions estimates. The evidence on spatiotemporal distribution of road traffic injuries also notes that RTIs mainly occur in economically developed provinces such as Zhejiang and Jiangsu [N7-R3], implying regional concentration rather than uniformity.

Methodological assumptions used in road vehicle estimates are clear from the evidence on emissions inventory methods. The evidence on stationary-source emissions guidance notes that stationary-source emissions are estimated according to reporting requirements, while mobile-source emissions guidance provides methods for estimating emissions for mobile sources [N6-R3][N6-R2]. The seasonal vehicle study further shows that emission rates can vary by fuel type and by season, supporting the use of activity-based or time-based modeling to capture traffic intensity changes [N2-R1].

In short, the China-specific road vehicle emissions profile is dominated by motorcycles, private cars, light-duty vehicles, buses, trucks, and rural vehicles, with diesel and gasoline vehicles contributing differently. Emissions are highest in winter and lowest in summer, and the methodological baseline is activity-based calculation using emission factors, fuel consumption, and seasonal traffic patterns [N2-R2][N2-R5][N6-R2][N6-R3][N8-R2].

direct comparison framework for agricultural machinery vs. road vehicles

A direct comparison of agricultural machinery and road vehicles is possible, but the evidence indicates important limitations. The common metrics for comparison are well established in the emissions literature: tons CO2e, PM2.5, and NOx [N1-F1][N2-R5]. For agricultural machinery, the evidence explicitly reports NOx and PM emissions from tractors and combine harvesters, with tractors accounting for 59.0% and 60.1% of total NOx and PM emissions from agricultural machinery in 2018, respectively [N1-F1]. For road vehicles, the evidence notes that emissions peak in winter and are lowest in summer, and that China IV vehicles have the highest emission contribution rates, ranging from 32.5% to 44.9% [N2-R5]. It also reports seasonal vehicle emission rates by fuel type during holiday and non-holiday periods [N2-R1]. These metrics are therefore compatible, but the two source categories differ in scale and operational context.

Conversion from activity-based estimates to emissions is a central methodological bridge in the evidence. The evidence on activity-based emissions calculation explains that activity-based emission factors multiply a physical unit of activity by an emission factor expressed in the same unit [N8-R2]. It also notes that activity-based methods use real-world operational data, such as litres of fuel burned, to calculate emissions with precision [N8-R5]. For agricultural machinery, this means that machine hours or fuel consumption can be multiplied by emission factors to estimate CO2e, PM2.5, and NOx emissions [N8-R2][N8-R5]. For road vehicles, the same logic applies: traffic volume, fuel consumption, and vehicle type can be converted into emissions using emission factors or traffic-activity-based estimates [N8-R2][N2-R2]. The evidence also indicates that emissions inventories for mobile sources are estimated using emission factors and activity-based methods, which is important for comparison [N6-F3].

Limitations of comparing different source categories are substantial. First, agricultural machinery and road vehicles are fundamentally different in operation mode and fuel use: agricultural machinery is off-road, typically diesel-powered, and tied to crop cycles; road vehicles are on-road, with a broader fleet composition and more diverse fuel use [N1-F1][N2-R2]. Second, the evidence shows that emissions vary by equipment category and vehicle class, so a single average factor may mask large differences [N1-F1][N2-R5]. Third, the evidence on emissions inventory methodology notes that power-based methods can introduce uncertainty when applied to individual machinery types, and that real-world performance can differ from bench-test results [N1-F1]. For road vehicles, seasonal and regional differences further complicate comparison, as emissions peak in winter and are lowest in summer [N2-R5][N7-R4]. Finally, the evidence on emissions factors and reporting methods distinguishes stationary-source from mobile-source emissions, which is important because agricultural machinery is a mobile source, while stationary sources are treated separately in inventory compilation [N6-F3].

In conclusion, the direct comparison framework is feasible using tons CO2e, PM2.5, and NOx as common metrics, with activity-based conversion from operational data to emissions [N8-R2][N8-R5]. However, the comparison should be treated cautiously because the two source categories differ in operation mode, fuel use, equipment composition, and seasonality, and because emissions inventories may use different methodological assumptions and emission factors [N1-F1][N2-R5][N6-F3].

## Integrated final answer: How do emissions from agricultural machinery in China compare to those from road vehicles during the peak agricultural season?

The evidence provided supports a nuanced comparison: **agricultural machinery and road vehicles emit differently in China, with tractors and combine harvesters dominating agricultural emissions, while road vehicles are a much larger and more heterogeneous fleet**. During the peak agricultural season, both systems intensify operation, but agricultural machinery emissions are more operationally and seasonally concentrated around planting and harvesting windows, whereas road vehicle emissions are shaped by broader seasonal traffic patterns and fuel-use behavior. The comparison is also limited by methodological differences and the distinct operational contexts of the two source categories [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R5][N6-F3].

---

## 1) What the evidence says about agricultural machinery emissions in China

### Dominant machinery types
The China-specific agricultural machinery emissions profile is dominated by **tractors and combine harvesters**. A 2022 study tested 39 typical agricultural machines in China, including 30 tractors and 9 corn combine harvesters, under real-world working conditions [N1-F1]. The same source reports that tractors accounted for **59.0% of NOx emissions** and **60.1% of PM emissions** from agricultural machinery in 2018, while combine harvesters accounted for **4.8% of NOx** and **3.4% of PM** emissions in the same year [N1-F1]. This makes tractors the largest contributors, but combine harvesters are still significant, especially during harvesting operations.

### Fuel use and engine efficiency
Agricultural machinery in China is heavily diesel-powered, with diesel engine power accounting for **77.6% of total mechanical power** in the 2019 China Agricultural Machinery Industry Yearbook [N1-F1]. This is consistent with the evidence that diesel engines are characterized by high engine power and low fuel consumption [N1-F1]. However, emissions vary by equipment category and operation type: a **rototilling tractor** produced significantly higher CO, NO, and PM2.5 emission rates than tractors used for field transportation, fertilizing, straw chopping, and straw mulching [N1-F1]. Similarly, grain combine harvesters were found to emit more than corn combine harvesters [N1-F1]. These differences suggest that engine efficiency and operating load are important drivers of emissions.

### Seasonal variation
The evidence on peak agricultural season timing points to **early summer**, specifically **May 5th as Lixia**, the seventh solar term, signaling peak growth season [N4-R3]. While the evidence does not provide a detailed seasonal emissions profile for agricultural machinery alone, it does show that fieldwork is **time-driven**, with work time determining required power and operational intensity [N5-F2]. The 2014 study used sowing and harvesting times for wheat, corn, and rice to build a national-level agricultural machinery emission inventory [N1-F1]. This implies that emissions intensity rises during planting and harvesting windows, but the evidence is thin on exact seasonal emissions variation for agricultural machinery.

---

## 2) What the evidence says about road vehicle emissions in China

### Fleet composition and fuel distribution
China’s road vehicle fleet is large and diverse, with vehicles classified into six categories: **motorcycles, private cars, light-duty vehicles, buses, trucks, and rural vehicles**, and two fuel types: **gasoline and diesel** [N2-R2]. The evidence also notes that **China IV vehicles** have the highest emission contribution rates, ranging from **32.5% to 44.9%** [N2-R5]. This suggests a fleet composition skewed toward older, more polluting vehicles and a strong role for diesel in the on-road fleet.

### Seasonal trends
Seasonal trends in road traffic and emissions are clear: emissions **peak in winter** and are **lowest in summer** [N2-R5]. Another source notes that seasonal vehicle emission rates vary by fuel type during **holiday and non-holiday periods** [N2-R1]. Road traffic injuries in China were also highest in **summer and autumn**, lowest in **February**, with rural areas and men disproportionately affected [N7-R4]. While this is about injuries rather than emissions, it reinforces that traffic intensity and risk vary seasonally and regionally.

### Methodological assumptions
The evidence on emissions inventory methods distinguishes **stationary-source** emissions from **mobile-source** emissions [N6-R3][N6-R2], which is important because road vehicles are mobile sources. The evidence also shows that emissions estimates often rely on **emission factors** and **activity-based calculation methods**, where activity data are multiplied by emission factors [N6-F3][N8-R2]. This means road vehicle emissions estimates are typically derived from traffic volume, fuel consumption, and vehicle composition rather than a single fixed factor.

---

## 3) How peak agricultural season affects machinery versus road traffic hours

The seasonal operational intensity comparison shows that **both systems intensify during peak season**, but in different ways.

### Agricultural machinery
Agricultural machinery intensifies during planting and harvesting windows, which are time-driven and tied to sowing and harvesting schedules [N5-F2][N1-F1]. The evidence indicates that fieldwork is driven by available work time, and that crops must be harvested within a few days of ripening [N5-F2]. This means agricultural machinery hours rise sharply during the peak agricultural season, which directly increases emissions.

### Road traffic
For road traffic, the evidence points to higher intensity in **summer and autumn** and a peak in **winter emissions** [N2-R5][N7-R4]. This mismatch means that road traffic intensity does not always align with agricultural seasonality. Summer and autumn are busy for road travel, but winter is the peak for emissions, likely because of colder weather, reduced vehicle efficiency, and heavier traffic demand [N2-R5].

### Regional and crop-specific variation
The evidence suggests regional variation in road traffic: **RTIs mainly occur in economically developed provinces such as Zhejiang and Jiangsu** [N7-R3]. For agriculture, the evidence implies that emissions intensity varies by crop cycle, since the 2014 study used sowing and harvesting times for wheat, corn, and rice to build an inventory [N1-F1]. However, the evidence provided is thinner for detailed regional comparisons in agriculture than it is for road traffic.

---

## 4) How operational intensity translates to emissions load

Operational intensity translates to emissions load through the **activity-based conversion logic** in the evidence. The evidence on activity-based emissions calculation explains that activity-based emission factors multiply a physical unit of activity by an emission factor expressed in the same unit [N8-R2]. It also notes that activity-based methods use real-world operational data, such as **litres of fuel burned**, to calculate emissions with precision [N8-R5]. This means that the more intense the operation, the higher the activity level and the greater the emissions load.

For agricultural machinery, higher operational intensity during peak season means more machine hours, more fuel burned, and therefore more emissions [N1-F1]. For road vehicles, higher traffic intensity means more vehicles on the road and higher overall emissions, even if the peak agricultural season is in summer [N2-R5][N7-R4].

A direct comparison is possible using the following common metrics: **tons CO2e**, **PM2.5**, and **NOx** [N1-F1][N2-R5]. ## 6) Limitations of comparing agricultural machinery and road vehicles

A direct comparison has important limitations. Finally, the evidence distinguishes **stationary-source** from **mobile-source** emissions, which is important because agricultural machinery is a mobile source, while stationary sources are treated separately in inventory compilation [N6-F3].

---

## 7) Bottom line

During the peak agricultural season in China:

- **Agricultural machinery emissions are concentrated in tractors and combine harvesters**, with tractors dominating NOx and PM emissions [N1-F1].
- **Road vehicle emissions are shaped by a large, diverse fleet and seasonal traffic patterns**, with emissions peaking in winter and lowest in summer [N2-R5].

This suggests that tractors are the largest contributors, but combine harvesters remain significant, especially in harvesting operations.

Fuel use and engine efficiency by equipment category are tied closely to emissions intensity. The evidence indicates that diesel engines are widespread in agricultural machinery because they are characterized by high engine power and low fuel consumption [N1-F1]. Similarly, grain combine harvesters were found to emit more than corn combine harvesters [N1-F1]. These differences suggest that engine efficiency and operating load matter, with higher-intensity operations leading to worse emissions performance.

Seasonal variation in operation intensity and emissions is less directly specified in the evidence, but the context provided by the peak agricultural season is important. ## 1) What the evidence says about agricultural machinery emissions in China

### Dominant machinery types
The China-specific agricultural machinery emissions profile is dominated by **tractors and combine harvesters**. A 2022 study tested 39 typical agricultural machines in China, including 30 tractors and 9 corn combine harvesters, under real-world working conditions [N1-F1]. Similarly, grain combine harvesters were found to emit more than corn combine harvesters [N1-F1]. These differences suggest that engine efficiency and operating load are important drivers of emissions.

### Seasonal variation

While the evidence does not provide a detailed seasonal emissions profile for agricultural machinery alone, it does show that fieldwork is **time-driven**, with work time determining required power and operational intensity [N5-F2]. The 2014 study used sowing and harvesting times for wheat, corn, and rice to build a national-level agricultural machinery emission inventory [N1-F1]. This implies that emissions intensity rises during planting and harvesting windows, but the evidence is thin on exact seasonal emissions variation for agricultural machinery.

## 2) What the evidence says about road vehicle emissions in China

## 1) What the evidence says about agricultural machinery emissions in China

### Dominant machinery types
The China-specific agricultural machinery emissions profile is dominated by **tractors and combine harvesters**. A 2022 study tested 39 typical agricultural machines in China, including 30 tractors and 9 corn combine harvesters, under real-world working conditions [N1-F1]. The same source reports that tractors accounted for **59.0% of NOx emissions** and **60.1% of PM emissions** from agricultural machinery in 2018, while combine harvesters accounted for **4.8% of NOx** and **3.4% of PM** emissions in the same year [N1-F1]. This makes tractors the largest contributors, but combine harvesters are still significant, especially during harvesting operations.

### Fuel use and engine efficiency
Agricultural machinery in China is heavily diesel-powered, with diesel engine power accounting for **77.6% of total mechanical power** in the 2019 China Agricultural Machinery Industry Yearbook [N1-F1]. This is consistent with the evidence that diesel engines are characterized by high engine power and low fuel consumption [N1-F1]. However, emissions vary by equipment category and operation type: a **rototilling tractor** produced significantly higher CO, NO, and PM2.5 emission rates than tractors used for field transportation, fertilizing, straw chopping, and straw mulching [N1-F1]. Similarly, grain combine harvesters were found to emit more than corn combine harvesters [N1-F1]. These differences suggest that engine efficiency and operating load are important drivers of emissions.

### Seasonal variation
The evidence on peak agricultural season timing points to **early summer**, specifically **May 5th as Lixia**, the seventh solar term, signaling peak growth season [N4-R3]. While the evidence does not provide a detailed seasonal emissions profile for agricultural machinery alone, it does show that fieldwork is **time-driven**, with work time determining required power and operational intensity [N5-F2]. The 2014 study used sowing and harvesting times for wheat, corn, and rice to build a national-level agricultural machinery emission inventory [N1-F1]. This implies that emissions intensity rises during planting and harvesting windows, but the evidence is thin on exact seasonal emissions variation for agricultural machinery.

---

## 2) What the evidence says about road vehicle emissions in China

### Fleet composition and fuel distribution
China’s road vehicle fleet is large and diverse, with vehicles classified into six categories: **motorcycles, private cars, light-duty vehicles, buses, trucks, and rural vehicles**, and two fuel types: **gasoline and diesel** [N2-R2]. The evidence also notes that **China IV vehicles** have the highest emission contribution rates, ranging from **32.5% to 44.9%** [N2-R5]. This suggests a fleet composition skewed toward older, more polluting vehicles and a strong role for diesel in the on-road fleet.

### Seasonal trends
Seasonal trends in road traffic and emissions are clear: emissions **peak in winter** and are **lowest in summer** [N2-R5]. Another source notes that seasonal vehicle emission rates vary by fuel type during **holiday and non-holiday periods** [N2-R1]. Road traffic injuries in China were also highest in **summer and autumn**, lowest in **February**, with rural areas and men disproportionately affected [N7-R4]. While this is about injuries rather than emissions, it reinforces that traffic intensity and risk vary seasonally and regionally.

### Methodological assumptions
The evidence on emissions inventory methods distinguishes **stationary-source** emissions from **mobile-source** emissions [N6-R3][N6-R2], which is important because road vehicles are mobile sources. The evidence also shows that emissions estimates often rely on **emission factors** and **activity-based calculation methods**, where activity data are multiplied by emission factors [N6-F3][N8-R2]. This means road vehicle emissions estimates are typically derived from traffic volume, fuel consumption, and vehicle composition rather than a single fixed factor.

---

## 3) How peak agricultural season affects machinery versus road traffic hours

The seasonal operational intensity comparison shows that **both systems intensify during peak season**, but in different ways.

### Agricultural machinery
Agricultural machinery intensifies during planting and harvesting windows, which are time-driven and tied to sowing and harvesting schedules [N5-F2][N1-F1]. The evidence indicates that fieldwork is driven by available work time, and that crops must be harvested within a few days of ripening [N5-F2]. This means agricultural machinery hours rise sharply during the peak agricultural season, which directly increases emissions.

### Road traffic
For road traffic, the evidence points to higher intensity in **summer and autumn** and a peak in **winter emissions** [N2-R5][N7-R4]. This mismatch means that road traffic intensity does not always align with agricultural seasonality. Summer and autumn are busy for road travel, but winter is the peak for emissions, likely because of colder weather, reduced vehicle efficiency, and heavier traffic demand [N2-R5].

### Regional and crop-specific variation
The evidence suggests regional variation in road traffic: **RTIs mainly occur in economically developed provinces such as Zhejiang and Jiangsu** [N7-R3]. For agriculture, the evidence implies that emissions intensity varies by crop cycle, since the 2014 study used sowing and harvesting times for wheat, corn, and rice to build an inventory [N1-F1]. However, the evidence provided is thinner for detailed regional comparisons in agriculture than it is for road traffic.

---

## 4) How operational intensity translates to emissions load

Operational intensity translates to emissions load through the **activity-based conversion logic** in the evidence. The evidence on activity-based emissions calculation explains that activity-based emission factors multiply a physical unit of activity by an emission factor expressed in the same unit [N8-R2]. It also notes that activity-based methods use real-world operational data, such as **litres of fuel burned**, to calculate emissions with precision [N8-R5]. This means that the more intense the operation, the higher the activity level and the greater the emissions load.

For agricultural machinery, higher operational intensity during peak season means more machine hours, more fuel burned, and therefore more emissions [N1-F1]. For road vehicles, higher traffic intensity means more vehicles on the road and higher overall emissions, even if the peak agricultural season is in summer [N2-R5][N7-R4].

---

## 5) Common metrics for comparison

A direct comparison is possible using the following common metrics: **tons CO2e**, **PM2.5**, and **NOx** [N1-F1][N2-R5]. The agricultural machinery evidence explicitly reports NOx and PM emissions, while the road vehicle evidence reports seasonal and fuel-type variations in emissions and notes that China IV vehicles have the highest emission contribution rates [N2-R5]. The evidence also shows seasonal vehicle emission rates vary by fuel type during holiday and non-holiday periods [N2-R1]. These metrics are therefore compatible, but the two source categories differ in scale and operational context.

---

## 6) Limitations of comparing agricultural machinery and road vehicles

A direct comparison has important limitations. First, the two source categories are fundamentally different in operation mode and fuel use: agricultural machinery is **off-road**, typically diesel-powered, and tied to crop cycles; road vehicles are **on-road**, with a broader fleet composition and more diverse fuel use [N1-F1][N2-R2]. Second, emissions vary by equipment category and vehicle class, so a single average factor may mask large differences [N1-F1][N2-R5]. Third, the evidence on emissions inventory methodology notes that **power-based methods** can introduce uncertainty when applied to individual machinery types, and that real-world performance can differ from bench-test results [N1-F1]. For road vehicles, seasonal and regional differences further complicate comparison, as emissions peak in winter and are lowest in summer [N2-R5][N7-R4]. Finally, the evidence distinguishes **stationary-source** from **mobile-source** emissions, which is important because agricultural machinery is a mobile source, while stationary sources are treated separately in inventory compilation [N6-F3].

---

## 7) Bottom line

During the peak agricultural season in China:

- **Agricultural machinery emissions are concentrated in tractors and combine harvesters**, with tractors dominating NOx and PM emissions [N1-F1].
- **Road vehicle emissions are shaped by a large, diverse fleet and seasonal traffic patterns**, with emissions peaking in winter and lowest in summer [N2-R5].
- **Both systems intensify operation during peak season**, but agricultural machinery intensifies around planting and harvesting windows, while road traffic intensifies in summer and autumn and peaks in winter [N5-F2][N7-R4].
- **A direct comparison is feasible using tons CO2e, PM2.5, and NOx**, but it should be treated cautiously because the two source categories differ in operation mode, fuel use, equipment composition, and seasonality [N1-F1][N2-R5][N6-F3].

In short, agricultural machinery emissions are operationally focused and seasonally concentrated during planting and harvesting, while road vehicle emissions are broader, more fleet-dependent, and heavily influenced by winter weather and seasonal traffic behavior. The comparison is useful, but the evidence supports a cautious interpretation rather than a simple “which is worse” conclusion [N1-F1][N2-R5][N6-F3].
